#298. Chelsea searches for new manager as Premier League breaks record for most sackings in a single season

It was just six months ago that Graham Potter was deemed the man to usher in a fresh, exciting era at Chelsea.

The club’s new ownership group, led by American businessman Todd Boehly, had enticed Potter away from Brighton with the promise of managing one of the most lucrative teams in world soccer.

More than $600 million was spent on bringing big-name players to the club and Potter, one of the most exciting young managers in the Premier League, was to mold them into a winning machine.

Chelsea has spent over $600 million on new signings. Here's why that's significant

But, on Sunday, the club announced that it had sacked its manager after an underwhelming spell in charge.

Potter managed to win just 10 of the 28 league matches this season and leaves the team 11th in the Premier League table.

In recent weeks, players had looked a shadow of their former selves and many fans had lost confidence that Potter’s plan for the club could ever work.

Eventually, after previously sticking by its manager, Blues ownership agreed.

“On behalf of everyone at the club, we want to thank Graham sincerely for his contribution to Chelsea,” the club’s co-owners Todd Boehly and Behdad Eghbali said in a statement.

“We have the highest degree of respect for Graham as a coach and as a person. He has always conducted himself with professionalism and integrity and we are all disappointed in this outcome.”

In his previous role as Brighton manager, Potter was given time to stamp his identity on the squad.

The club was punching above its weight financially and, as a result, carefully selected new signings which would compliment Potter’s style of play.

The approach paid off as the team became an established Premier League outfit which has gone on to greater things this season – the Seagulls currently sit sixth in the league and in the UEFA Conference League qualification spot.

At Chelsea, it seemed the complete opposite.

As was the case under previous owner Roman Abramovich, the club expected instant results and used its financial weight to sign a number of high-profile names, including the likes of Enzo Fernández and Mykhailo Mudryk.

Despite his impressive CV, Potter had never managed superstars and suddenly found himself in a changing room with multiple.

The scatter gun approach to recruitment also left the team lacking balance and organization with Potter failing to get a tune out of a team busting with talent.

In truth, many had raised an eyebrow when Potter, inexperienced at the very top level, was chosen to replace Thomas Tuchel as manager.

Despite falling out of favor with fans by the end of his tenure, Tuchel had guided Chelsea to the Champions League title in 2021 and is still considered by many as one of the best coaches in the world.

The German has gone on to sign with Bavarian giant Bayern Munich through the 2024/25 season and recently told reporters he needed “quite a bit of time to distance himself from Chelsea” because leaving the club had hurt him.

Bayern Munich sacks manager Julian Nagelsmann, appoints Thomas Tuchel

“Todd [Boehly] said he would be different to Roman [Abramovich],” former Liverpool player and current pundit Jamie Carragher wrote on Twitter.

“I feel for Graham Potter, but it was inevitable. You don’t change Tuchel for Potter. Ridiculous decision to start with.”

With 10 games left in the league and a Champions League quarterfinal against Real Madrid on the horizon, Chelsea still has plenty to play for.

Assistant coach Bruno Saltor will take over on an interim basis, but Boehly and his team must now look for a long-term replacement capable – and willing – to bring order to Chelsea’s chaos.

Potter’s sacking is yet another sign of just how transient managers can be in the top-flight of English football, especially when results aren’t instantaneous.

There has now been a record 12 sackings in the Premier League so far this season, with Potter leaving his position the same day Leicester boss Brendan Rodgers was sacked from his.

The previous record was 10 manager changes in a single season, set in four other campaigns, most recently in 2017/18.

#296. How to watch videos on Apple CarPlay while parked

It's straightforward enough, but requires the right apps (and a compatible car).

CarPlay brings your iPhone apps right to your car's dashboard. However, not every app gets a CarPlay version — it's mostly limited to audio, messaging and navigation apps. But with iOS 27, users can finally watch videos on CarPlay when they're parked. But watching videos on CarPlay has certain limitations, and it's not just about running the latest iOS.

For one, not all video apps support CarPlay right now. Even if they do, the feature only works in vehicles with "video-in-car" technology, which helps CarPlay detect when the car is stopped. The bad news is that even Apple doesn't have a list of vehicles compatible with video apps on CarPlay, so you'll have to find out for yourself whether yours is. Still, if you're lucky enough to have a compatible vehicle, here's how to watch videos on CarPlay.

Right now, few video apps are compatible with CarPlay. Some of the most popular ones, like YouTube or Netflix, don't support it natively yet. If you have a compatible video app on your iPhone, you'll see it on CarPlay's Home Screen. In that case, just open the app to browse the video catalog. There's no need to find the video on your iPhone or stream it via AirPlay. When you start driving, CarPlay automatically switches to audio-only mode, so you can keep listening to the rest of a podcast, for example.

Luckily, CarPlay also supports AirPlay, so you can stream a video from your iPhone or iPad to your car's dashboard even if an app doesn't work with CarPlay just yet. With your iPhone connected to CarPlay, open an AirPlay-compatible app (like YouTube) and start playing a video. Then, look for the AirPlay button and choose CarPlay from the list. You should then see the video on your car's dashboard, with playback controls on both your iPhone and CarPlay. To bring the video back to your iPhone, tap the AirPlay button again and deselect your car. Also, make sure your car is parked; otherwise, it won't play the video.

If you've tried the steps above and still can't watch videos in your car with CarPlay, it's most likely because your car doesn't support it. Automakers need to add support for video apps, and many older car dashboards don't support it and probably never will. Apple requires CarPlay screens to be at least 1,920 x 1,080 pixels to play video. CarPlay systems also need to support the HEVC codec and at least 4GB of memory, which older systems may lack.

You'll also need up-to-date software. AirPlay to CarPlay requires iOS 26.4 or later, while native video apps are only available on iOS 27. If you haven't updated, open your iPhone's Settings and go to General, then Software Update to check whether any updates are available. iOS 27 is available for the iPhone 11 and later, so your iPhone most likely supports it.

If your car isn't compatible with CarPlay video, brands like Carlinkit and Ottocast sell Android-based "AI boxes" for your car's dashboard. These let you install Netflix, YouTube or pretty much any other video app without jailbreaking your iPhone. Be aware that these workarounds will also bypass the restrictions that limit video playback to when the vehicle is parked, and that watching video on the road can be distracting.

#294. 5 things you didn't know Steam's overlay could do

You might think you know Steam's overlay, but there's a lot more hiding behind that Shift + Tab shortcut.

Back in 2023, Valve updated Steam to release, among other new features, a redesigned overlay you can access while playing your favorite games. While nearly every publisher and storefront now offers some form of overlay in their games and launchers, for my money Steam has them all beat with its breadth of options. If you're a Steam user and don't use the built-in overlay frequently or at all, you might be surprised by all the things it can do.

If you're new to Steam, you can open the overlay in-game by pressing Shift and Tab on your keyboard at the same time. If you want to change the shortcut, you can do so from Steam's options menu, which you can access by clicking Steam at the top left of the interface, followed by Settings and then In-Game. You'll also find other handy settings here, such as the option to disable the overlay altogether. This is also a good place to mention that Steam will remember how you've configured your overlay for each individual game, so there's no need to activate, arrange and resize parts of the interface every time you go play your favorite titles.

When you bring up the overlay, you'll find shortcuts for all the features I mention below along the bottom of the interface. Simply press one of them to bring up the feature you want to use.

I know what you're thinking: can't you just Alt-Tab out of a game to open your browser? While you certainly could do that, I find switching to Steam's built-in browser is a lot smoother since it's integrated directly into Valve's client. It's a great way to check something, such as how to tackle a quest you're having trouble with, without taking yourself out of a game completely. I'll also mention here that you can access Steam's often excellent community guides directly from the overlay, making them easy to reference, especially if you favorite one.

If you're playing a puzzle game like Blue Prince or Tunic, being able to jot down notes as you try to piece together clues can make things so much easier. Steam's built-in text editor is fairly robust, allowing you to format text and write code blocks.

I don't know about you, but my gaming time is limited most days. I try to get around that by sneaking in gaming sessions whenever I can, which means I often only have 45 minutes or an hour before I need to be doing something else. For that reason, I find using the overlay to keep track of time and set timers really helpful.

Again, you could just use your smartphone to do that, but the beauty of doing things this way is you don't need to look at your phone. Bonus tip: you can pin any element of the overlay so that it appears in-game. This is particularly handy to do with the timer. And don't worry, if you do pin something, it won't appear in any screenshots you take directly through Steam.

Since Steam is not just a platform for playing games on your own, the overlay has a couple of features that are great for sharing your favorite games and moments with your friends.

I mentioned screenshots before. You can view any images or recordings you've made through the overlay, even ones you've captured in other games. If you click on a screenshot and select Share, you can save it to a folder on your computer or send it to one of your Steam friends over chat. You can even send your screenshots and recordings directly to your phone via the Steam Mobile app (Android and iOS). As you can imagine, this is a great way to share your gameplay to social media.

If you're not familiar with Remote Play Together, it's a Valve protocol that allows you to play local co-operative games with your friends for free over the internet. With most connections, up to four people can join in the fun. As long as a game supports the protocol, your friend doesn't need to own the game. You can share control of your keyboard in case your friend doesn't have a controller of their own. And don't worry, they can't access any other part of your PC while Remote Play is active. In any case, the Steam overlay is a great place to start a co-op session. Just click the Remote Play button and invite your friends.

Paris Saint-Germain’s miserable season went from bad to worse on Sunday as the team suffered a second straight home defeat with a 1-0 loss to Lyon.

Even before the game kicked off, Lionel Messi bore the brunt of the frustrations of some PSG fans who whistled when his name appeared on the big screen during the announcement of the starting lineup.

Lionel Messi passes 100 international goals with hat-trick against Curaçao

After Alexadre Lacazette missed a first-half penalty, Bradley Barcola’s goal 10 minutes into the second period was enough to earn Lyon the three points on a night that PSG rarely looked like threatening the visiting goal.

Lens’ 1-0 victory over Rennes and Marseille’s 1-1 draw with Montepellier means both teams are now just six points behind PSG at the top of Ligue 1, and even the domestic title may slip from the team’s grasp.

The reaction of some fans on Sunday must have felt a world away from the adulation and worship Messi received during his recent return to Argentina for friendlies against Panama and Curaçao as the country continued its World Cup celebrations.

Messi’s arrival at the Parc des Princes was supposed to be the missing piece that would help PSG finally win the Champions League, the trophy the club’s Qatari owners crave the most.

Messi has 34 goal contributions in all competitions for PSG this season – 18 goals and 17 assists – second only to Mbappé’s 38 and head coach Christophe Galtier refused to lay the blame for the team’s failures at the Argentine’s feet.

“We can’t expect everything from Leo and Kylian,” he added.

“Paris’ problem is when the No. 1 objective of the Champions League is no longer accessible, it seems that the season no longer exists – and at all levels,” he told reporters.

What's the best iPhone to buy right now? This fall, that question got a lot more interesting.

In mid-September, Apple launched the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max with upgraded cameras, a revamped vapor chamber cooling system, longer battery life, and a fresh, AI-ready chipset. A month later, it released the long-awaited iPhone Duo, its first-ever foldable. Mashable senior editor Stan Schroeder deemed it "the most exciting iPhone since the first one."

The new Apple phones join the standard iPhone 17, the budget iPhone 17e, and the super-slim iPhone Air to round out the 2026 iPhone roster, which now runs on iOS 27. We've tested the entire iPhone family, and we've compared them all to pick the best iPhone for every type of user.

Apple's smartphones have never been more powerful, feature-rich, or diverse in their form factors. Alas, they've also never been pricier. Every current iPhone has gotten more expensive due to the ongoing global memory crisis, which has jacked up the cost of electronic components over the past year. (The Duo turned out to be slightly less of a splurge than the gossip mill predicted, though it's still the most expensive iPhone ever.) Unfortunately, there's no escaping higher prices with any other brand: All the best smartphones have seen price increases this year.

So, is it worth splashing out on the Duo or one of the new Pro models? Or would you be perfectly happy with something less snazzy and more wallet-friendly, relatively speaking? After extensively testing every single iPhone, Mashable's experts have recommendations for all budgets and usage needs.

One more thing: Before you buy your new iPhone, be sure to check out our coverage of the latest carrier deals. If you trade in an older device and sign up for a new line or data plan, you could pay a fraction of the price — or nothing at all.

Who it's for: In all likelihood, you. We think the iPhone 17 is the model most people should buy. It's also the most colorful iPhone on the market.

The new iPhone 18 Pros and iPhone Duo are amazing phones, but they're overkill for the average user. Last year's iPhone 17 is still the most well-rounded, "just right" phone in Apple's lineup. (We don't expect the new base model iPhone 18 to land until spring 2027.)

The iPhone 17 is a fast-enough, long-lasting-enough, nice-looking-enough smartphone that feels "Pro" where it counts for most people. Namely, it has a 120Hz, always-on display and an ultrawide camera with a dedicated macro mode, but none of the extra photography or thermal fixings intended for superusers. Compared to the budget iPhone 17e, which costs $200 less, it has a brighter, smoother screen, nicer cameras, and 15 percent more battery life.

Was the iPhone 17 an earth-shattering upgrade over the iPhone 16? Not really, but it got better in some crucial yet practical ways without straying over the $1,000 mark. Mashable's Schroeder christened it "the most compelling standard iPhone in years."

#291. Re-releases of Wing Commander, Ultima titles hit Steam and GOG

It’s mostly bad news from EA lately, but preservation efforts are nice to see.

Many people are not big fans of game publisher EA right now for good reason, but for those who remember a better time in the 1990s, there’s a little good news. Twenty-five classic games from that EA era have been lightly remastered and updated, then placed for sale on Steam and GOG, including several Wing Commander games and nearly the entire Ultima series.

Below is the full list of remastered or re-released games:

In a lengthy blog post published this week, Jim Vessella, a senior producer at EA, described the efforts that went into remastering Wing Commander I-IV and Prophecy, Privateer 2, and Road Rash.

It’s a long, detailed story that’s worth reading yourself, but here’s a top-level summary. After working on the mostly widely acclaimed Command & Conquer: Remastered Collection in 2019, Vessella writes that he learned about and visited a room at EA’s Redwood Shores campus that contained a large archive of poorly labeled or sorted physical media from ages past.

In his free time, and with the help of others, he began cataloging this archive and discovered, among other things, that it contained virtually the entirety of the original masters of Wing Commander III and Wing Commander IV‘s full-motion-video cutscenes.

The story that ensues involves building a small team of contractors, poring through the footage 17 hours a day on swing shifts to label and digitize it, and then coordinating with several key community members—particularly Matt Wells, who has made community enhancement patches for some of the Wing Commander games—to put together remasters of those games.

The flagship offering of those remasters is much, much higher-quality full-motion video sequences than have ever been available before, but other enhancements include 60 frames-per-second gameplay, a plethora of newly available .INI tweaks, and full controller support (though looking at the Steam forums for the games, some folks are having trouble with said controller support).

For Privateer 2—the little-remembered sequel to Wing Commander: Privateer—the crew couldn’t find the original, high-quality remasters of the FMV scenes, and ended up getting in touch with the game’s original cinematics director, Steve Hilliker, who had the tapes in his attic. Hilliker had always wanted to take a new color-grading pass, and he did just that, while also remastering and upscaling all of the cutscenes.

Similar updates were given to Wing Commander Prophecy. The blog post also details GOG’s involvement in restoring and remastering Prophecy and Road Rash. For the latter, EA re-licensed the entire original soundtrack for re-release.

The e collection is on sale on GOG and Steam right now; previous owners of the old versions of the games on GOG and the EA storefront get these remasters for free. None of the games cost more than $5 each.

One good story doesn’t undo a lot of bad news and questionable decisions from EA, but this shows that a few passionate people can do something remarkable for game preservation, even if some of the work was done on a volunteer basis outside normal working hours. (EA committed some resources to the restorations as the project progressed, though.)

While the remasters aren’t perfect, the gaming industry could use news like this. It’s worth reading the full story in the blog post for a journey down memory lane and a look at how involved a restoration process like this can be.

#290. How a bottleneck calculator for your GPU and CPU works

They're a quick way to help you check component compatibility before you build or upgrade a system.

Troubleshooting computer components can be daunting. After the physical labor of installing a new part, you'll want to stress-test it to make sure your replacement works properly. Finding a faulty part is relatively straightforward, but what if the component is limiting the rest of your system? During a stress test, you might see your CPU at 100 percent while your GPU is practically idling.

This is considered a bottleneck. When one component holds back the rest of the system, it hinders performance until you resolve the bottleneck. For example, if your CPU is at 100 percent while your GPU is barely drawing power, we'd classify that as a CPU bottleneck since it's impairing your GPU's performance. Knowing which component is bottlenecking your system helps you decide what to upgrade or troubleshoot next. Before you buy a new GPU or any expensive component, check for bottlenecks first.

Some websites and software offer bottleneck calculators to help you troubleshoot these issues without stress-testing your system. While they can help you quickly spot a hardware mismatch, they're rarely accurate. Many online calculators can't tell the full story of how your system behaves. That said, a bottleneck calculator can help you check component compatibility before you build or upgrade a system, saving you valuable time while troubleshooting.

A bottleneck calculator takes your chosen CPU and GPU and compares their performance at your target resolution— common test outputs are 1080p, 1440p and 2160p. If both components are rated to perform adequately at your target benchmark, you'll receive a bottleneck score around ten percent or less. However, if one component is ill-equipped to handle the benchmark, it will receive a high percentage, indicating it's a bottleneck. The lower the percentage, the better the score.

Typically, the CPU is the culprit behind most PC bottlenecks. The CPU's job is to send information to the rest of your system in a timely fashion. If it's too slow, other components will wait for the CPU to finish. This is usually what causes stutters in video games. However, if your GPU is hovering around 95 percent usage while struggling to render the application, you may have a GPU bottleneck; GPUs tend to struggle when rendering graphics well above their intended resolution or frame rate. A bottlenecked GPU can cause screen tearing, low frame rates and inconsistent performance.

That is why bottleneck calculators ask for your target resolution: your GPU's performance depends heavily on how many pixels it renders each second. Paradoxically, this clinical approach to calculating performance is what makes bottleneck calculators so unreliable: they rely on spec sheets and theory, not real data from your PC.

Bottleneck calculators can't give you truly accurate data because of how they work. Since they reference manufacturer spec sheets, they omit variability from other system components and the application(s) you're testing. Not every graphics card is made equal, just as not every video game uses your GPU as effectively. A newer Intel GPU may struggle to run an older DX11 application that most Nvidia or AMD cards would run flawlessly. A powerful workstation CPU like the Ryzen 9 7950X won't perform as well as many X3D Ryzen chips for gaming because they have smaller L3 caches. These nuances are completely lost in these bottleneck calculators.

While they may not be ideal for detailed system troubleshooting, bottleneck calculators help with system-build planning. They're a convenient way to quickly check if your chosen CPU and GPU can handle your target resolution out of the box. They can also be a fun way for hobbyists to check strange hardware combinations you wouldn't normally see.

But for those looking for accurate tests on their PC hardware, performance monitoring software will always yield more reliable results. Bottleneck calculators can't account for your installed drivers, background apps you should disable, or performance issues in the game you're benchmarking. A simple bottleneck percentage doesn't tell the full story.

#287. How to set up SpaceXAI's Grok in Google Workspace (and what it can do)

A free add-on puts Musk’s chatbot inside Google Docs, Sheets and Slides.

If you've been on X recently, you've probably noticed people (or bots) tagging Grok under posts to fact check a claim or generate an image, but most Google Workspace users have no idea that Grok can now work inside Docs, Sheets and Slides, too. SpaceXAI released a free Grok add-on for Google Workspace in July 2026, and getting it running is a matter of just a few clicks. Install it once from the Google Workspace Marketplace, open it via the Extensions menu in whichever app you're working in and off you go.

That one installation covers all three of Google's Workspace editors, with Grok opening in a side panel next to the file rather than in a separate tab. It's the same spot where you'll find Google's Gemini panel. From there, Grok can answer questions about a spreadsheet and highlight the cells it used, turn an outline into a slide deck and knock rough notes into a formatted doc. While it's free and easy to insert Grok into your workspace, there are some factors worth considering before rolling out the welcome mat.

Grok is listed on the Google Workspace Marketplace and is free to install. Open it, click Install and choose the Google account you want to use, then click Continue. If you'd rather not leave the file you're in, you can also install Grok directly from inside Docs, Sheets or Slides by navigating to Extensions > Add-ons > Get add-ons. Workspace admins can also deploy it across an entire org.

Clicking Continue brings up Google's permission screens. Grok will ask for see, edit, create and delete permissions for all Google Docs files and every Slides presentation in your account, even if you're installing it from within an individual file. It has narrower access to Sheets, covering only those that the add-on has been installed in, and its overall Drive access only stretches to files you use with Grok. It'll also ask for permissions to connect to an external service, which allows Grok to send what it reads to SpaceXAI.

Once Grok is installed, open any doc, spreadsheet or presentation and nav to Extensions > Grok > Open Grok to bring up the side panel. You'll then be prompted to Get Started and sign in. Once authenticated, Grok will be accessible and usable across all three Workspace apps.

Grok can write directly onto the page in Google Docs, doing all the things you'd expect an LLM to do, such as turn rough notes into a draft with proper docs headings and lists. However, when I asked it to turn notes on installation instructions into a draft, the results were AI slop. Grok's changes show up as visible revisions in Google Docs version history and, with Grok's connectors switched on, it can apparently pull in context from recent emails or files in Google Drive. I personally wasn't willing to give it that level of access to my emails or files and hooked it up to my secondary spam Gmail and Workspace account instead.

In Slides, Grok can build a presentation deck from an outline and add new slides that match the existing theme, researching the topic from the Web or from X (though that doesn't seem like a great idea, in my opinion.) To its credit, SpaceXAI's use cases page has some fairly interesting examples to borrow as prompts. I asked Grok to build a six-slide deck based on its track record for accuracy and political bias since 2025, with cited sources on every slide and concluding with a rating of how reliable Grok is as a source.

In Sheets, Grok can read whatever ranges you select, answer with citations, point to specific cells, write formulas into the formula bar and insert charts. It can also rerun scenarios when you change an assumption, with each change being implemented as an ordinary edit that can be undone later.

Google's Gemini chatbot is built into Workspace by default and opens from the Ask Gemini icon at the top-right of Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive and Chat. But it's not free: Work accounts need an eligible Workspace plan, while personal accounts need a Google AI Plus, Pro or Ultra subscription.

Grok costs nothing to add, and it's the only one of the two that pulls research from X into whatever you're generating, but whether that's a plus or not is certainly debatable. Gemini integrates with more apps than Grok, and it can be run in Gmail, Drive and Chat, while Grok is restricted to Docs, Sheets and Slides. However, you can get around this somewhat and give Grok access to gmail and Drive files via connectors. If you don't pay for Gemini, Grok is the simplest free way to get an AI side panel into Google Workspace, but only if you're comfortable with giving it the access it asks for. If you already have a Gemini subscription or access via work, there's little point using Grok unless you especially want it to cite information from the cesspit that is X.com.

#283. You can easily keep your home network running during a power outage — here's how

Stay online when the power goes out with the right backup hardware and a little planning.

If your power goes out, your laptop's battery will keep it up and running. It's a convenience that's not afforded to every electronic in your home. For example, networking gear, like a Wi-Fi mesh system or, more importantly, your router, will go dead silent in the event of an outage.

If you're on, say, an important video call for work, losing your connection could make for a rude interruption. It's even worse if you're mid-game, about to score that critical victory and secure bragging rights. Fortunately, there's an easy way to prevent interruptions in the event of a complete power outage.

The first step to keeping your network running in a power outage is a quick checkup on your networking equipment. If any of the devices between the wall jack and your laptop lose power, your connection goes with them. So, you'll want to understand that chain if you don't already. For cable internet, that means a modem and router, or a single gateway device that handles both.

If you have fiber internet, you'll have a router and an optical network terminal (ONT), or the box where the fiber line enters your home. Some providers install a battery backup on the ONT, although these are usually aimed at phone lines, not necessarily your internet connection. So check with your internet provider if you aren't sure.

Keep in mind that if your fiber ONT and router are in different rooms, you'll need two separate backup power units (or one with a long extension cord).

An uninterruptible power supply (UPS) is the best way to keep your internet up and running during a power outage. These devices sit between the power outlet and your networking gear, automatically switching to battery when your home's power goes out.

Like most products, they come in a range of prices. A modest one that can keep a router running for an hour or longer costs well under $100. More expensive models can last longer and even handle more power-hungry devices, like a PC.

It's worth doing a quick test run. Unplug the UPS from the wall when nobody at home is using the internet, and make sure everything stays online. If it does, you're ready for the next outage.

If you already own removable batteries for things like power tools and cordless vacuums, there's a cheaper option. You can buy small inverters compatible with your battery brand, whether it's DeWalt, Milwaukee or Ryobi.

There is a big downside. Unlike a UPS, inverters don't switch your networking gear over to battery power automatically, so you'll need to plug in the networking gear when the power goes out and wait for your equipment to restart. But on the positive side, inverters do let you swap batteries in and out if you get stuck in a longer outage.

As long as you supply the batteries, you can find inverters for as little as $30 for third-party models.

With a backup power source, it's easy to get carried away with keeping unessential devices working. However, whichever backup power option you use, plug in only your networking equipment; this isn't the place for your TV or game console.

And of course, this advice only applies to power outages where your internet provider's connection stays up. Your best option for a complete internet outage is your phone's mobile hotspot or a mobile hotspot device.

#282. Ships loiter near subsea cables amid Iran's warnings to Trump

Iran threatened to attack subsea cables if US escalates military strikes again.

Several tanker ships linked to Iran have been loitering over subsea Internet cables in the Gulf of Oman near the Strait of Hormuz—a possible indication that the Iranian government is preparing to attack such undersea infrastructure in response to any renewed US and Israeli strikes.

The movements of three sanctioned tankers and an Iranian fishing boat have been tracked near major undersea cables by the maritime intelligence firm Windward in October, according to the Financial Times. Six active cables currently cross through the contested Strait of Hormuz, linking the Middle East to Europe, Africa and Asia, with two more cables having segments under construction in the region.

Four countries, including Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar, depend entirely upon such subsea telecommunications connections running through the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint to link with the outside world. But other countries also depend heavily on the region’s undersea cable network—one third of India’s westbound Internet traffic goes through the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.

One cable under construction, the 2Africa cable, is owned by a tech consortium that includes the US company Meta. That was one of the major cable corridors visited by the drifting Iran-linked ships.

Windward used both ship-tracking data and satellite images to track the vessels as they slowed down and looped around near multiple cables, with some ships then “going dark” by switching off their automatic identification system (AIS) transponders that normally broadcast their location and other information.

Such movement and behavioral patterns suggest the Iran-linked ships may be “mapping the cable routes, or placing charges or mines on them while dark,” Windward told the Financial Times.

Windward highlighted the examples of two sanctioned tankers linked to Iran that spent days drifting “directly over regional cable corridors… both with no commercial reason to stop” in a blog post on October 26. Both ships carried no commercial cargo.

Since the US and Israel first launched a major war with Iran in February 2026, Iran’s response beyond targeting US military bases, ships and aircraft has included attacking commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and hitting oil refineries and other energy infrastructure along with airports in various Gulf countries.

Iran has also made a point of threatening or attacking US Big Tech infrastructure in the Middle East, including launching multiple drone strikes on Amazon data centers. In May 2026, a spokesperson for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Iran would “impose fees on Internet cables” belonging to US tech companies and other owners.

But more recently, multiple Iranian officials and commanders of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) have warned that they could directly attack the undersea cables running through the Strait of Hormuz. This came after President Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to renew major US military strikes on Iran and warned he could “annihilate” the country during a speech at the United Nations in New York on September 22.

“Seven major cables run through the Strait of Hormuz, supporting global Internet operations and commercial data transmission,” one IRGC spokesperson said on October 20. “We remind the enemy of this.”

The latest phase of the war has involved more limited US military strikes against Iranian targets, even as Trump has alternated between threats and touting the possibility of a diplomatic breakthrough. Meanwhile, Iran has increased drone strikes and other attacks on commercial ships to exert its own pressure on the United States, with October marking the highest number of ship attacks since the war began.

Much damage has already been done. The limited fleet of cable-laying ships used for installation and repair has not been able to venture safely into the region since the war began, which forced the Meta-backed 2Africa cable to pause its planned expansion. The war has also compelled US tech companies and Gulf countries to accelerate efforts to develop alternative cable routes bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.

The Middle East is not the only part of the world where threats to the Internet’s undersea backbone have intensified. Subsea infrastructure is increasingly at risk from sabotage and gray-zone warfare from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific Ocean.

#281. Exercise coaching boosts colon cancer survival

Evidence suggests exercise can keep more cancer patients alive. But what does "living longer" actually mean, and who does it apply to?

In 2025, an international trial found that people treated for colon cancer were more likely to be alive eight years later if they had received long-term exercise coaching.

The question facing doctors now is less whether people with cancer should exercise, and rather how they should build it into routine care.   In the US, that shift is reaching hospital standards. From January 2027, breast cancer centers must screen patients' physical function and recommend exercise or physical therapy where needed.

Yet experts caution that the trial's findings may not apply to every cancer or every patient.

The 2025 trial, called CHALLENGE, was led by the Canadian Cancer Trials Group. It began enrolling patients in 2009 and published its results in 2025.

The trial's 889 participants came from six countries, most from Canada and Australia. All had finished surgery and chemotherapy for stage 2 or 3 colon cancer, which had not spread to distant organs.

Half received only health education materials on exercise and healthy eating. The other half additionally met a physical activity consultant for three years.

In the exercise group, the target was similar to adding 45 to 60 minutes of brisk walking, three to four times a week. The amount and type of activity varied from person to person, said Tormod Skogstad Nilsen, a cancer exercise researcher in Norway. But he said participants achieved lasting increases in their physical activity.

Exercise helped. People in the exercise group were less likely to see their cancer come back, to develop a new cancer or to die. In all, 93 had at least one of these setbacks, compared with 131 in the health education group.

In cancer research, living longer usually means a larger share of people is still alive at a given point. It does not promise anyone a set number of extra years.

Eight years after joining CHALLENGE, about 90 of every 100 people in the exercise group were alive, compared with about 83 of every 100 in the health education group. That is about 7% more people alive in the group who had guided exercise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For people without cancer, the evidence comes from studies that follow people's habits and health over many years. These can show a link, but not prove cause and effect. Active people may also eat better or smoke less.

In another 2025 study, more than 85,000 adults in the United Kingdom wore a wrist tracker for a week. Over about six years, those who moved most had a 26% lower risk of 13 cancers, including breast and colorectal cancer, than those who moved least.

Even light activity, such as household chores, was linked to lower risk. The link held after researchers accounted for lifestyle, weight and other health conditions.

Earlier research, based on people's self-reporting, has led to similar conclusions. A 2016 analysis of 1.44 million adults in the US and Europe linked free-time activity to a lower risk of many cancers, largely regardless of weight or smoking.

A trial to prove prevention is unlikely: Many cancers take years to develop, so it would need huge numbers of people followed for a long time.

CHALLENGE included only people with colon cancer. But how it picked participants offers a clue: Before joining, they had to pass a fitness test.

Anna Campbell, a professor of clinical exercise science at Edinburgh Napier University in Scotland, sees that as a guide.

"I think patients with any other cancer stage II and III who have a reasonable baseline level of fitness and no major comorbidities that would prevent them from undertaking moderate to vigorous activity could be considered for similar interventions," she said. Comorbidities are other health conditions.

Nilsen noted some people decline to join exercise trials because they feel too unwell or tired, or do not want to exercise. "Hence, study populations are typically younger, 'healthier', and most times slightly more motivated compared to a clinical population," he said.

The coaching aimed to make activity a lasting habit, and Campbell said that is where the trial's value lies.

"The main success of the study is that it enabled the participants to become independent exercisers staying active in a safe and effective and individualized way," she said.

Nilsen agreed. Helping people become more active "in their own environment," without depending on a well-equipped training center, "would likely lead to more sustainable activity behavioral changes," he said.

He is wary of fixed targets, however. "Exercise should be tailored to each individual and the challenges they face, rather than striving to reach a given minimum of exercise required," though health care resources may not always allow it, he added.

In a 2024 survey of 549 people with cancer, only one in 10 had been referred to an exercise service. Yet almost three in four thought their oncologist should raise the subject.

"There are some excellent examples of effective pathways but these are few and far between," said Campbell. Good services bring everyone on board, from surgeons to community fitness instructors.

"Ideally, one person in the clinical setting needs to champion the program to link all the team together."

Campbell expects CHALLENGE's regular coaching will be cut back in everyday care. Apps and live online group sessions could still work, she said, if run by properly trained staff.

One recent study of live online exercise engaged patients from poorer backgrounds, in rural areas and with advanced cancer. "It answered some of the barriers, such as cost, travel and lack of confidence," she said.

Patients can ask their care team what exercise is safe for them and what support exists.

According to Nilsen, a training session can bring structure and company. "You made it here, despite your feeling unwell or fatigued this morning, so you feel mastery based on that," he said.

#278. How to connect an Apple Pencil to your iPad

Getting your Apple Pencil linked with your iPad is easy, as long as they're compatible.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Contrary to the impression Apple gives, you don't need an Apple Pencil to use an iPad. As input accessories go, you're probably better off picking up a keyboard and mouse for your iPad first. But with a giant touchscreen, illustration and handwritten notes are obvious selling points, and you need some sort of stylus to make that work. The company is naturally going to upsell you on its own accessories, regardless of whether cheaper alternatives might get the job done.

Pairing an Apple Pencil to an iPad is dead simple, for the most part. But there is a process, plus surprising compatibility issues can crop up. You'd think a stylus would be one of the simplest accessories possible, but Apple's evolving iPad ambitions have created a few roadblocks.

We'll also deal with a few general troubleshooting issues, though chances are that you'll be up and drawing within a few minutes.

The exact pairing process depends on the Pencil model you own. In the case of the USB-C Apple Pencil, slide open the end of the stylus to reveal the USB-C port, then connect it to your iPad using an appropriate cable. A pairing prompt should appear on-screen, at which point all you need to do is hit Tap to Connect. As a bonus, your Pencil will charge at the same time. This also works with the iPhone Duo, which is only compatible with the USB-C Pencil.

The process is even simpler with the Apple Pencil Pro. Once you've unboxed it, let it clip magnetically to the long side of your iPad. That's it — you're ready to go in seconds. This is also how you charge the Pencil Pro, and how you'll likely store it most of the time unless you're worried about it being knocked off inside a bag or suitcase. Meanwhile, the second-generation Pencil pairs just like the Pro.

If you've got a first-gen stylus, you'll need to remove its cap, plug it in via its Lightning connector, then tap Pair. In case you're using the original Pencil with a USB-C base iPad (either the 10th gen or A16 model), you'll need a Lightning to USB-C adapter.

Unfortunately, the first-gen model and USB-C Pencil must be re-paired every time you restart your iPad or disable Bluetooth.

Your first concern is those compatibility issues we mentioned. The first-gen Pencil is intended for Lightning-equipped iPads; it won't work with newer USB-C iPad mini, Air or Pro models. The base iPad models from 2022 and 2025 support it with an adapter. Meanwhile, the second-gen Pencil is limited to certain iPad models that aren't too old or new.

The USB-C Pencil is more broadly supported, while the Pencil Pro only works with a narrow slice of iPad Air, Mini and Pro models. It's smart to check Apple's Apple Pencil compatibility list to confirm, especially if you're planning to buy a new iPad or Pencil.

If your Pencil pairs but is still having trouble, physically reconnect it to your iPad. Once that's done, restart your iPad by holding down a volume button and the power button, then swiping the power-off slider when it appears. Hold the power button again after a moment to turn it back on. (On an older iPad with a Home button, just hold the power button.) Update your iPad at Settings > General > Software Update too.

Try re-pairing your Pencil, which may involve physically disconnecting the stylus from your iPad first. If nothing's working, navigate to Settings > Bluetooth and double-check that Bluetooth is enabled. If your Pencil already shows as Connected, tap the i icon next to it, then Forget this Device. Retry the appropriate pairing process.

In some circumstances, it may be that your Pencil doesn't have enough power to pair, so simply leaving it plugged in for a while could do the trick. Apple also suggests removing any cases or covers from your iPad on the off chance they're interfering. But if you've reached that level of desperation, you'll probably need to book a service appointment at your local Apple retailer, hopefully covered by AppleCare.

#277. Chinas moon plan mirrors NASAs, except for one big difference

China's plan to land people on the moon by 2030 mirrors NASA's on paper but skips crewed lunar test flights, trusting robotic rehearsals for its first human landing instead.

Chinese space officials laid out their approach at the 7th Manned Space Symposium in Beijing on Oct. 31, according to Xinhua, the Chinese government's wire service. A slide reportedly from the presentation posted by CNSpaceflight, an independent outlet that tracks the Chinese space program, shows two of the initial missions with nobody aboard. A crew flies the Mengzhou, or "Dream Vessel," capsule to Earth orbit in 2027. Then the robots take over. The Lanyue, or "Embracing the Moon," lander touches down on its own in 2028, and an uncrewed mission rehearses the full landing sequence in 2029.

"For any crewed mission, we will try to fly it in an unmanned state first," said Wang Xiang, chief designer of the Chinese lunar exploration program, in the English captions of a CCTV report, China's state-run broadcaster.

The split cuts to the heart of a heated new space race and reveals two different institutional cultures. China's tight-lipped, military-run program trusts machines to prove its lunar hardware works. NASA's civilian program, working in public view to land astronauts first in 2028, leverages human test pilots. U.S. leaders say they're reviving the Apollo playbook that beat the Soviet Union to the moon: put crews on key test flights, launch often, and build on each mission.

"It's not entrepreneurial thinking or tech industry pixie dust or some new management philosophy," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman at a news conference on Oct. 23. "It's a playbook this agency knows really well — the same playbook that went from Apollo 7 splashdown to Apollo 11 in just nine months."

NASA has already flown one of those crewed test flights. Artemis II sent four astronauts around the moon in April. Next year, the four-person Artemis III crew will spend about two weeks in Earth orbit practicing maneuvers to dock the Orion spaceship with test versions of two commercial landers.

One lander is from Blue Origin, and the other is from SpaceX. Astronauts will climb into Blue Origin's lander to check its air and life-support systems, but will only briefly dock with Starship.

Earlier this year, NASA decided to do that test as a separate mission, shoehorned between Artemis II and the first crewed moon landing. If something goes wrong, "we can come home much more quickly," explained Jeremy Parsons, who manages NASA's Artemis program.

Apollo followed roughly the same script. Four crewed test flights came before Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed in July 1969. China's first crew to head for the moon will be the one that lands.

Despite this major difference between the plans, NASA will lean on some robotics, too. SpaceX aims to land an uncrewed Starship on the moon by the end of 2027, and Blue Origin is working on its own uncrewed demonstration after Artemis III. NASA will keep both landers in the running as long as possible before picking one for its first crew, while China is building a single lander.

In other ways, the two plans look alike. Two Long March-10 rockets will launch China's capsule and lander separately, and the pair will link up in orbit around the moon. Two of the three crew members will then ride the lander to the surface and back. NASA's Orion carries four astronauts but also sends just two down. Blue Origin's lander even follows China's route, flying to lunar orbit on its own to meet the crew. SpaceX breaks the pattern, docking its Starship with Orion near Earth and pushing the spaceship to the moon.

Want more science and tech news delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for Mashable's Top Stories newsletter today.

China says its uncrewed flights will make the first crewed landing safer. Its robotic lander also will gather some scientific data, measuring how hot the lunar surface gets and how the dust behaves. Its 2029 rehearsal will run every step, from docking in lunar orbit to landing, lifting off and docking again. The program has already completed early tests of its rocket, capsule, and lander.

The race, Isaacman warned, "will be much closer than it ever needed to be," emphasizing that China has the spacecraft, landers, and a "credible two-launch architecture" to put taikonauts, the Chinese term for astronauts, on the moon within three years.

NASA's own deadlines have slipped repeatedly. Artemis first aimed for a 2024 landing, and Isaacman recently acknowledged that Artemis III was running about three months behind schedule.

He conceded that urgency has its limits: "No amount of my enthusiasm or schedule pressure changes the laws of physics."

#276. Is AMD's Ryzen 7 5800X3D CPU still worth buying in 2026?

If you already own an AM4 system, one of AMD’s more affordable Zen 3 CPUs might be a better option.

Thanks to the Sam Altmans of the world, the price of consumer memory, including RAM and solid-state storage, has become prohibitively expensive. Just 16GB of DDR5 RAM can now set you back as much as $300, making new AM5 and LGA 1851 PC builds unobtainable for most people. In fact, the price of memory has gotten so bad that AMD brought back its flagship AM4 gaming processor, the Ryzen 7 5800X3D, just to give those still on an AM4 system a way to upgrade their PC.

But should you buy a 5800X3D in 2026? Let's take a look at some of the factors you should consider before deciding to spend $349 on a previous generation CPU.

I bought my 5800X3D in July 2023, or a year after it first went on sale in 2022. I've already gotten three years of use out of the 5800X3D, and can't complain about its gaming performance. If you came here looking for benchmarks, I'll point you to outlets like Hardware Unboxed that have done extensive testing of the rereleased 5800X3D. What I can offer instead are anecdotes from a few recent games.

I've been playing a lot of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered. While the original is now more than 11 years old, the remaster incorporates a new, optional ray-tracing pipeline that can be very demanding, even on the most powerful of modern PCs. Additionally, with the game's next-gen update in 2022, CD Projekt Red added new "Ultra+" options for all of the game's original graphics settings that were designed to scale its visuals to newer hardware. Specifically, there's one setting in particular that can tank your frame rate if you're running an older CPU.

That option is "number of background characters," which controls how many NPCs the game will render to fill out the game's settlements. If you push this setting to Ultra+ in Novigrad, the Witcher 3's largest city, you will see a staggering number of NPCs wandering its streets. Some older AM4 CPUs, including the venerable Ryzen 5 3600, can struggle in this scenario. The 5800X3D handles it with ease, however.

Without frame generation, my 5800X3D and Radeon RX 9070 can maintain a solid 80 to 90 frames per second at 1440p with ray-traced global illumination and ambient occlusion enabled. In the few hours I've spent questing through Novigrad, my 1 percent lows never dipped below 70 frames per second.

My experience in the Witcher 3 is representative of what I've seen in many other recent games, including Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2, Marathon and Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced. I'm able to play all of them at frame rates that either nearly or fully saturate my 165Hz display. The best thing I can say about the 5800X3D is that in all the years I've owned it, I've never regretted buying it.

Whether it makes sense for you to buy the 5800X3D in 2026 is a different question. As of September 2026, the AM4 socket is now 10 years old, and despite an incredible run, it is effectively a dead platform. AMD will not release any new, more powerful AM4 processors. Therefore, traditional wisdom would tell you to upgrade to a new AM5 or LGA 1851 system because those are current platforms where you could get future upgrades down the line. At least that would be the advice I would give someone if the AI boom hadn't made DDR5 RAM unaffordable.

A scan of Newegg shows a 32GB kit of 6,000MHz, CL30 memory from Corsair going for nearly $600 at the time of writing. If GPU prices weren't also out of control, you could buy an entire video card for that same amount of money. If you're still running an AM4 build, the 5800X3D can be tempting since you re-use the RAM you already own. But before you go out and buy one, there are a few questions worth asking yourself.

First, if you're unhappy with your PC's gaming performance, have you thought about first upgrading your GPU instead? I know that sounds like a crazy suggestion when memory pricing has had a significant knock-on effect on the cost of video cards, but the reality of PC gaming is that no component will more greatly impact your gaming experience than a better GPU.

Even with a CPU bottleneck, a faster, more powerful graphics card will reduce your system latency. Obviously, you don't want to upgrade to a GeForce RTX 5080 if you're running a Ryzen 5 3600, but buying one of AMD's recent GPUs, like the RX 9060 XT or RX 9070, could make more sense than upgrading to the 5800X3D. A major benefit of this approach is that you can bring your new GPU over to whatever AM5 or LGA 1851 rig you build in the future. The same is not true of the 5800X3D.

If you do decide to take this approach, I strongly recommend going with an AMD GPU instead of a NVIDIA one. Relative to their Team Red counterparts, NVIDIA video cards typically require a more powerful CPU to get the most out of them due to the overhead NVIDIA's Game Ready drivers impose on processors.

That said, if you don't want to upgrade your GPU right now, the good news is an AM4 system can greatly benefit from a drop-in CPU upgrade. Hardware Canucks recently tested the Ryzen 5 5500, which you can frequently find on sale for less than $100, against the older Ryzen 5 2600X. Paired with a recent GPU, the newer processor delivers a significant performance uplift.

In Cyberpunk 2077 Phantom Liberty, for instance, the 5500, paired with a RX 9070, put up an average frame rate of 102, with 1 percent lows of 72.9. By contrast, the older 2600X, using that same GPU, averaged 85.7 frames per second, dipping to 55.8 frames per second for its 1 percent lows. That increase in 1 percent lows is massive. It's the difference between a game that feels smooth and one that feels jittery.

If you're on an older Ryzen chip like the 2600X or 3600, the 5800X3D will be a major upgrade for you, but I bring up the Ryzen 5500 to point out you don't need to spend the $349 AMD is charging for its most powerful AM4 CPU. The 5500, alongside the 5600X and 5700X, are all great, more affordable alternatives that you can get for less than $150. The 5800X3D is honestly overpriced for a processor that's four years old, especially considering it sometimes went on sale for $300 or less before AMD first discontinued it. Not to sound like a broken record, but money you save on a CPU can be put toward a more powerful GPU, and there's no sense in pairing the 5800X3D with a mid-range GPU like the RTX 5060 Ti or RX 9060 XT.

The scenario where it might make sense to upgrade to the 5800X3D is if you already own 32GB of 3,200MHz or 3,600MHz DDR4 RAM. Since replacing that much high-performance memory with the equivalent amount of DDR5 RAM would easily cost you $500 or more, the 5800X3D is a relative bargain in that context. And with neither AMD nor NVIDIA expected to release their next generation of GPUs until late 2027 or 2028 at the earliest, there's a possibility the 5800X3D could carry through to the end of that generation. Alternatively, if you already own a high-end GPU like the RTX 5070 Ti or 5080 and have it paired with a less powerful AM4 CPU, the 5800X3D would allow you to get the most out of one of those graphics cards.

#275. What to know about the IIHF Women's Ice Hockey World Championship

As ice hockey's governing body continues to wrangle over how to respond to a CAS order to reinstate Russia to international play, the top women's tournament gets underway in Denmark without Russia.

Since its inception in 1990, the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship has almost always been held in the spring — apart from 2021 and 2022, when the COVID-19 pandemic saw it moved to the summer. This year, though, the tournament, being hosted by Denmark from November 6 to November 16, is being held in November for the first time. The idea is make it easier for all of the world's best players to participate. Since its inception in 2023, the North America-based Professional Women's Hockey League (PWHL), widely considered the world's best, has had to pause its season to allow players to take part in the Worlds. This is no longer necessary, as the PWHL's regular season doesn't open until December.

"This gives the women's game a unique selling point," International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) President Franz Reindl recently told the SID news agency. "Because the PWHL season begins after this, we can be certain that the very best players are participating."

Previously, the teams were divided into a stronger group and a weaker group, with the idea being to avoid, as much as possible, lopsided scores. This is because women's hockey is not as balanced as the men's game, with Canada or the United States having won every tournament since its inception. Under the old system, all five teams in the stronger Group A advanced to the quarterfinals. Under the new format, four of the five teams advance from both groups. This also sees the two powerhouses, the USA and Canada in separate groups, meaning the marquee matchup can't occur early in the tournament.

Group A: USA, Czechia, Switzerland, Germany, Austria

Group B: Canada, Finland, Sweden, Japan, Denmark

No. While the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled on October 30, 2026 — a week before the opening faceoff of the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship — that the IIHF must allow Russia back into its tournaments during the 2026-2027 season, it made no mention of this tournament. Under the CAS ruling though, the IIHF will be required to include Russia at the 2027 tournament in Quebec City.

As noted above, either Canada or the United States has won every edition of this tournament – and indeed the two countries have split Olympic gold medals between them (Canada 5, USA 3) since the sport was introduced to the Winter Games in 1998. There is nothing to suggest that this is about to change in Herning and Esbjerg, although Canada enters the tournament with a vastly different roster from the one that won Olympic silver in Milano in February. Among those looking to break this North American domination are Finland, the only other team ever to have made it to a World Championship final and Switzerland, who took bronze in Milano.

The United States and Canada are having to play in generic kits provided by the International Ice Hockey Federation's official supplier due to an ongoing commercial rights dispute. The Canadian federation, Hockey Canada, said in a statement on Wednesday that its players would be wearing jerseys designed by True Hockey instead of their Bauer jerseys featuring the national team logo. USA Hockey has confirmed that its players too will be wearing jerseys without its national emblem.

"While we have yet to see the jersey Canada will be playing in on Friday, our team remains focused on the tournament and representing our country proudly on and off the ice,” Hockey Canada said.

#273. Musk's Twitter promised a purge of blue check marks. Instead he singled out the New York Times

Some VIP Twitter users woke up on Saturday expecting to have lost their coveted blue verification check marks in a previously announced purge by Elon Musk. Instead, Twitter appeared to target a single account from a major publication Musk dislikes and changed the language on its site in a way that obscures why users are verified.

Twitter had said it would “begin winding down” blue checks granted under its old verification system — which emphasized protecting high-profile users at risk of impersonation — on April 1. In order to stay verified, Musk said, users would have to pay $8 per month to join the platform’s Twitter Blue subscription service, which has allowed accounts to pay for verification since December.

But one high-profile account did lose its blue check over the weekend: the main account for the New York Times, which had previously told CNN it would not pay for verification.

William Shatner is mad he may have to pay to keep his blue Twitter checkmark. Elon Musk says too bad

After an account that often engages with Musk posted a meme this weekend about the Times declining to pay for verification, Musk responded in a tweet saying, “Oh ok, we’ll take it off then.” Musk then lashed out at the Times — just the latest instance of the billionaire slamming journalists or media outlets — in a series of tweets that claimed the outlet’s coverage is boring and “propaganda.”

The weekend moves are just the latest example of Twitter creating confusion and whiplash for users over feature changes — and in this case, not just any users, but many of the most high-profile accounts that have long been a key selling point for the platform. It also highlights how Musk often appears to guide decisions about the platform more by whims than by policy.

Although the New York Times’ main account lost its blue check, its other accounts, such as those for its arts, travel and books content, remained verified. (It’s not clear why the New York Times doesn’t have a gold “organizations” check mark, like accounts for other news outlets, including the Associated Press and the Washington Post.) After its blue check was removed, a spokesperson for the New York Times reiterated to CNN that it does not plan to pay for verification.

Twitter, which laid off most of its public relations staff last fall, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a separate puzzling move, Twitter’s blue bird logo at the top of the site was replaced on Monday with doge, the meme representing the cryptocurrency dogecoin, which Musk has promoted. The price of dogecoin shot up 20% on Monday.

Musk has been threatening to take away “legacy” blue check marks from users verified under Twitter’s old system since shortly after he bought Twitter last fall.

In early November, Twitter launched the option for people paying for its Twitter Blue subscription service to receive blue checks. The program was quickly put on pause after being plagued by a wave of celebrity and corporate impersonators, and was relaunched in December.

Twitter also rolled out a color-coded verification system with differently colored marks for companies and government entities, but Musk continued to say that individual users would eventually have to pay for blue checks.

In the days leading up to the blue check purge that wasn’t, prominent users such as actor William Shatner and anti-bullying activist Monica Lewinksy pushed back against the idea that, as power users that draw attention to the site, they should have to pay for a feature that keeps them safe from impersonation.

By muddying the reason accounts are verified, the new label could risk making it easier for people to scam or impersonate high-profile users. Experts in inauthentic behavior have also said it’s not clear that reserving verification for paid users will reduce the number of bots on the site, an issue Musk has raised on and off over the past year.

Musk, for his part, has previously presented changes to Twitter’s verification system as a way of “treating everyone equally.”

“There shouldn’t be a different standard for celebrities,” he said in a tweet last week. The paid feature could also drive revenue, which could help Musk, who is on the hook for significant debt after buying Twitter for $44 billion.

Musk last week also said that starting on April 15, only verified accounts would be recommended in users’ “For You” feeds alongside the accounts they follow.

–CNN’s Oliver Darcy contributed to this report.

#272. Doctors pull knife from man's eye that went through his brain—and he's fine now

It’s the exact path, not the apparent severity that matters most, doctors say.

A man in his 20s showed up to a UK hospital with the hilt of a knife sticking out of his face. The 15 mm-wide blade hidden within went completely through his right eye and through his brain, with the tip of the blade hitting the top of his skull.

Despite the ghastly injury, the man was alive and conscious when he arrived. He could still talk and move all four limbs. His doctors described him as being in a state of agitation. On the Glasgow Coma Scale, he scored a 12 (E3 V4 M5), indicating a “moderate” brain injury, just one point above “mild.” He could open his left eye when told, but otherwise kept it closed (E3 score); he could talk and answer questions, but was confused (V4); and he intentionally moved away when pressure was applied to his body (M5).

In a report published Friday in BMJ Case Report, his doctors said they were concerned that in his confused, agitated state he may try to pull the knife out on his own. So, they swiftly sedated and intubated him. They put him on prophylactic treatments for bacterial infections, including tetanus. Then they used images to see what was going on in his head.

The blade was entirely through the right eye socket and eyeball. It traversed the left frontal and temporal lobes of his brain, passing through in front of—and without apparently injuring—the corpus callosum, which connects the two sides of the brain and is full of nerve fibers. The blade also missed the left internal capsule, which holds another bundle of nerve fibers.

In terms of damage to major blood vessels, doctors found that the blade was close to the left internal carotid artery, a major blood vessel, but didn’t seem to have damaged it. Doctors did find, however, that a branch of the middle cerebral artery looked to be indented by the knife.

After consulting with various medical specialties, the man’s doctors moved to emergency neurosurgery. They opted to remove part of his skull to directly see into the brain, but used a conservative “pull-and-see” method to slide the blade out rather than invasively excavate it. After it was out, the doctors saw no signs of significant hemorrhaging. The brain wound was cleaned and drained before surgeons patched up his skull. His right eye, however, couldn’t be saved. Given its extensive damage, it was removed.

The man then moved to intensive care, where he recovered rapidly. A day after surgery, doctors were able to remove his breathing tube. He developed some minor right-side weakness, but it resolved two days later. Scans of his brain showed steady improvement—a little bleeding and swelling, and there was some air in his brain tissue from where the knife had been. But otherwise, it appeared to be healing. He developed no infections and had no seizures.

Despite the “dramatic intracranial trajectory,” his language function was preserved, and he had no loss of movement or coordination, they reported. He was discharged from the hospital and at follow-up appointments remained “neurologically well,” with ongoing eye and mental health care.

As for how the injury happened, his doctors still don’t know. “The mechanism is unclear,” they wrote. However, they noted he had a history of depression.

The doctors reflected on how lucky the man was to have survived and to have such a full recovery. Such injuries that go through the eye and the brain are rare. When they do occur, they’re usually from “high-velocity mechanisms” such as gunshots or other ballistic injuries. Knives, rods, and nails fit into the rarer “low-velocity mechanisms. “Such “low-velocity penetrating brain injuries carry substantial morbidity and mortality because of hemorrhage, vascular injury, abscess, meningitis, cerebrospinal fluid leak, seizures and neurological deficit,” they wrote.

But such fortunate recoveries aren’t unheard of; they cited reports of other remarkably unexpected recoveries from seemingly devastating brain injuries. That includes the famous case of Phineas Gage, a railroad foreman who survived an 1848 accident that sent a large iron rod directly through his head. The rod entered below his left cheekbone and exited the top of his skull. (Although he survived and recovered, Gage’s personality was said to have changed after the accident. The doctors in the knife-wound case did not mention any such personality changes.)

“Echoing classic and contemporary examples of severe frontal lobe penetration with unexpectedly preserved neurological function, including Phineas Gage and a reported nail-gun injury, this case highlights that outcome may depend less on external severity than on precise trajectory relative to critical vascular, cortical and subcortical structures,” the doctors concluded.

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#271. How long should a PC processor actually last?

If you treat it right, it should last until it's obsolete.

Building a new PC is a major investment, especially with prices of some components skyrocketing recently. Given the expense, it's natural to wonder not just if you can afford it now, but how long a PC should last if you do fork over the cash to build one. The central processing unit (CPU) is one of the biggest expenses in building a PC, but you likely won't need to buy a new one too often.

Under most conditions, you don't need to worry about your processor wearing out from regular use. Manufacturers don't list specific expected lifespans for their processors, but it's not uncommon for a CPU to remain functional for a decade or more after it's installed. Rather than your CPU failing, it's much more likely that you'll eventually want to replace it when it can't keep up with the new games or programs you use your PC for.

The most common time for a processor to fail is when it's still new. The manufacturing process can produce faulty CPUs from time to time, and when that happens, they'll likely give you trouble from the start. If you've had your CPU for a while, some of the signs that it's failing are your computer freezing for no clear reason, failing to boot or randomly restarting. All of these problems can be caused by other hardware, though, and pinning the problem to the CPU is as difficult as it is rare.

If your computer isn't performing as you'd like it to, it's worth checking if your CPU is just outdated. First, pull up your PC's Task Manager and check the Performance tab. Keep an eye on the CPU screen to see how much of the processor's power is being used. Under normal conditions, it should almost always stay below 20 percent. Some spikes are normal, but if it's constantly approaching its upper limits, you might want to consider an upgrade. Your CPU will be much more active during intensive tasks like gaming, but if it stays at 90 percent or more, especially if your GPU usage stays low at the same time, that could be cause for concern.

The biggest stressor to your PC is heat, which degrades performance of every component over time. The best thing you can do for your PC's longevity is to make sure it has adequate airflow by properly installing fans and regularly cleaning dust out of the case. Programs like HWiNFO let you monitor your system's temperature — if your CPU rises above 60 degrees Celsius under normal load or above 80 degrees during intensive tasks, it's worth looking into what improvements you can make. These numbers can vary based on the particular CPU, though, so it's best to follow manufacturer recommendations if they're available. If temperatures are high, you should also consider replacing the thermal paste on your CPU, which can last five years or more but eventually becomes less effective at regulating heat.

Overclocking your CPU — increasing its speed beyond the manufacturer's recomendations — can also reduce its lifespan, though usually it will still last until it's obsolete if you've overclocked safely. Other than time and heat, the most likely threat to your CPU is damage from a power surge or a faulty power supply. While rare, these are still more likely than a CPU simply "going bad" with age. It can be difficult to pinpoint exactly which component is failing without going to a professional technician, but with even minimal care, your CPU should keep ticking well past the point when it's time for an upgrade.
